speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Solicitor General. In view of the fact that he said outside the House yesterday that Roy Atkinson, president of the National Farmers' Union, had been under surveillance at one time by the RCMP, and this has been verified by a journalist who has a statement on tape from the travel agency to that effect, would the minister inform the House at this time of the reasons Mr. Atkinson was under surveillance at one time by the RCMP?

subsubtopic: REASON FOR SURVEILLANCE OF ROY ATKINSON
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I checked on this matter and I find that the RCMP did check with the Saskatoon travel agency to see if Mr. Atkinson was to travel to Prince Edward Island. At that time there was an interest in his activities, not on the basis of subversion or security but on the basis of information received that the National Farmers' Union were planning to illegally disrupt certain peaceful activities in PEI, such as the Charlottetown Old Home Week.

subsubtopic: REASON FOR SURVEILLANCE OF ROY ATKINSON
speechtext: Oh, oh!

The RCMP had been asked to find out if this information was correct and, if so, how many people were travelling from Saskatchewan to participate in these particular illegal activities.
I might say that the National Farmers' Union had previously been involved in certain massive tractor blockades in PEI and certain arrests had taken place and charges laid. So at the time the RCMP did check with this agency with respect to this possible disruption of peaceful activities in PEI. I might say that whatever was to take place did not take place and there have been no further checks on Mr. Atkinson since that time. That was the only time.

subsubtopic: REASON FOR SURVEILLANCE OF ROY ATKINSON

There was a tractor demonstration in August of 1971, and I found, on checking with Mr. Atkinson's lawyer this morning, that the charge against him under section 381 of the Criminal Code was conspiracy to intimidate the public from the

lawful use of a highway for no valid reason. The case was dismissed at a preliminary hearing in magistrate's court. I should like to know from the minister whether or not the only reason Mr. Atkinson was put under surveillance, was subversion or whether it was the intention to commit a criminal offence, to which he referred in the House. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct a question to the right hon. Prime Minister.
In view of the importance of this matter, especially for Quebecers, in view of the fact that yesterday the Prime Minister received a call from Mgr. Gregoire on the deportation of a certain number of Haitians, and since the Minister of Communications has stated to the press in a telephone interview that the cabinet has indeed undertaken to examine the possibility of deciding favourably on the Haitians' condition, could the Prime Minister advise us today whether the cabinet is still examining this matter and hoping to come with a solution which, as everybody is hoping, will protect completely the security of those Haitians?

subsubtopic: CONSEQUENCES FOR HAITIANS OF DEPORTATION-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as to the first part of the question, we certainly want the federal government to take the right solution to protect all the people involved, that is Haitians as well as Canadians themselves. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question.
Does the Prime Minister's reply mean that there are no changes possible to the decision already rendered and announced by the Minister of Manpower and Immigration? Since the act contains a special clause dealing with the persons concerning whom there are reasonable grounds to believe that they are likely to come to serious harm, could not the government avail itself of this clause, out of pity and for humanitarian reasons, to grant days of grace to the Haitians concerned, should it deem it necessary?

subsubtopic: CONSEQUENCES FOR HAITIANS OF DEPORTATION-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: It is precisely because of this clause that the minister and the government have made sure that each case will be heard and decided on its own merit. I do not understand what the hon. member means by more global solutions. The issue we are dealing with now is likely to come up over and over again, so that it is essential that the government and opposition members agree on procedures which are both fair and humanitarian.

subsubtopic: LOCAL INITIATIVES PROGRAM-ALLEGED REFUSAL OF PROJECTS APPROVED BY ADVISORY COMMITTEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to put a question to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration.
In connection with LIP projects, the department has asked us a few months ago to suggest the membership of advisory committees responsible for recommending projects to the department. Now I have been told that projects recommended by advisory committees in some constituencies are rejected by the department, while others recommended by political friends are accepted. I do not want to be partisan, but when it came to the membership of committees which we suggested, I did not ask myself whether they were Liberal, Progressive Conservative or Social Credit. speakeroldname: Hon. Robert K. Andras (Minister of Manpower and Immigration):
subsubtopic: LOCAL INITIATIVES PROGRAM-ALLEGED REFUSAL OF PROJECTS APPROVED BY ADVISORY COMMITTEES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am able to assure the hon. member that in principle this is not the case. When the department receives applications, some of them may not satisfy the initial criteria at all, that is, the criteria established for screening as to eligibility, but even those applications are forwarded, for information, to the constituency advisory group where such a group exists. The function of the advisory group is to examine these applications on the basis of community needs and of their suitability, and to recommend priorities within the budget allocation. I do not usually interfere if there is agreement that the project is eligible, if it has been approved by the constituency advisory group and if the hon. member involved has not made any particular or valid objection to it. In such a case it would be almost automatically approved subject to the budget available. If the hon. member has any instances of a specific nature to show there has been a departure from this process I would be very grateful if he would register them with me. I will follow through and find out what, and why, deviations, if any, have taken place.

speakeroldname: Mr. Andy Hogan (Cape Breton-East Richmond) moved:
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE LEADERSHIP IN SOLVING WORLD FOOD CRISIS
speechtext:
That this House condemns the government for its failure, both before and during the World Food Conference in Rome, to provide leadership concerning the food crisis facing many developing nations, and calls on the government to give real leadership on this most acute problem of our time by increasing its commitment of food and other agricultural assistance to such nations and by adopting a trade policy favourable to their future development.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in opening this debate on the world's food crisis and Canada's responsibility, I want to quote from a group of scientists and economists who met on the eve of the World Food Conference. This group was led by economist Barbara Ward, and this part of their statement puts the problem in the urgent perspective from which we must not hide, despite the natural human desire to put such urgent, depressing and complex problems from our minds. As someone has said, there is no subject, however complex, which if studied with patience and intelligence will not become more complex. I quote from the statement:
Even if official development assistance almost doubled by 1980, the poorest countries containing at least 20 per cent of all the world's

November 15, 1974
World Food Crisis
people are threatened with an actual decline in their already precarious living standard.
A panel of experts addressing the United Nations-spon-sored gathering at Rome put the urgency of the problem in the very short run, for the next eight or nine months, in even starker terms that we can all understand:
The primary question before us is how many of the world's people may not survive until the next harvest.
The Food and Agricultural Organization of the UN estimates the shortage in food grains as between 7 million and 11 million tons, broken down in this way: India, 3.4 to 7.4 million; Bangladesh, 1.9 million; Pakistan, 1 million; Sri Lanka, 200,000; and 20 other nations, mainly African, including the sub-Saharan section, 1.3 million.
I now want to make an evaluation of Canada's response to this need. We are now well aware of the essential response of Canada, made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen), at the World Food Conference. He promised, on behalf of Canada, one million tons of food grains for each of the next three years. The government House leader, in the absence of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, told us in the House a week ago last Wednesday that the countries at the Rome conference were asked to pledge a total of ten million tons of grain annually for three years. Canada has consented to contribute 10 per cent of that total.
The House leader said on that occasion that this would mean an "enormous increase" in money for food aid. He did not mention, though, that for this country's 180,000 wheat farmers, the 36.7 million bushels-which is the equivalent of one million tons a year-is worth about $940 to each of them in income. He also neglected to tell the House, of course, that Canada had contributed some 1.3 million tons of food aid, worth about $90.8 million, in 1970 when the world food crisis was not nearly as threatening. Our GNP was then $85 billion, and today it is in the vicinity of $120 billion. He mentioned that Canada would be prepared to increase substantially the allocation of commodities other than food grains. He did not mention, however, the steady sag in food aid by this federal government in the past four years.
The government House leader seemed euphoric and boastful in the House about Canada's contribution, but many of us found his attitude somewhat narrow and parsimonious, depicting sort of a complacent attitude, especially in view of the desperate seriousness of the world's pressing poverty problem. After all, the amount of wheat promised to the poor countries by us at Rome represents only half the amount of wheat we Canadians eat each year. A million tons of wheat makes enough flour to produce some 1.5 billion loaves of bread, or about three loaves for each of the some one-half billion hungry people in the world. Indeed, Canada's emergency food grains pledge works out to about one slice of bread per person every five days. So much for the question of immediate aid. What about helping them in the long run?
I want to speak about Canada and the fertilizer problem in the developing countries. The House leader did not mention anything about providing fertilizer to these needy countries. At present we are giving none. Many concerned and knowledgeable people insist that if we are serious in wanting to help solve the longer term crisis, we

will have to contribute at least 150,000 tons of fertilizer to these countries for at least 10 to 15 years, if they are to learn to feed themselves. One ton of fertilizer can produce
10	to 15 additional tons of grain in India and Bangladesh. The extent of the catastrophe facing the fertilizer industry in developing countries is scarcely believable. During the period 1965-71 the fertilizer industry in Canada, Japan and many western countries was plagued with overcapacity. This turned out to be a blessing for the least developed countries: they could buy low-priced fertilizer on world markets and this helped to make the so-called "green revolution" a reality.
By 1972, world demand had caught up with supply. The
011	price crisis of 1973 made things much worse for the very poor countries. Certain petroleum products, especially naphtha, have become the principle feedstocks for nitrogen fertilizer. Price increases in these petroleum products have thus led to. further price increases in fertilizer products. Canada can really help these countries develop their own food capacity by supplying them with elemental sulphur and potash, both basic raw materials for potassic fertilizer. We are one of the largest producers and exporters of potash in the world, as I recently found out during a visit to Saskatchewan. We also have an abundance of elemental sulphur in Alberta. The federal government should, for purposes of helping the least developed countries, subsidize both of these abundant commodities for export to these very poor countries.
If I can ever get your attention, Mr. Speaker, this should be clearly kept in mind while the federal and provincial government of Saskatchewan-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE LEADERSHIP IN SOLVING WORLD FOOD CRISIS
speechtext: Order, please.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE LEADERSHIP IN SOLVING WORLD FOOD CRISIS
speechtext:
I am sorry, Mr. Speaker. This should be clearly kept in mind while the federal and provincial government of Saskatchewan play tug-of-war over the question of taxation and royalties connected with the potash industry. Another alternative we can quickly look into, to help overcome the all but hopeless handicap of the poor nations with regard to fertilizers, is to use some of the extremely abundant, known coal reserves of Alberta- which compared to the reserves of Nova Scotia, from where I come, are minute-for the production of nitrogen fertilizer by means of a coal gasification process now being perfected in Alberta.
Alternatively, we can see if it is possible to help India test whether the Alberta technology for coal gasification can be used in turning India's large coal reserves to production of nitrogen fertilizer. I repeat, Mr. Speaker, if we are serious about helping these countries develop their own capacity to grow their own foods, we should sincerely and quickly consider these and other possible options.
Now I wish to speak for a few minutes about the priority in respect of food production-which should be present in this country and is not. It seems to me, though, as I mentioned in my maiden speech in the House, that over at least the next decade Canada has to build an almost new agricultural policy based on the premise that, while we cannot feed the world's starving, as one of the few grain exporting nations left we have to make a contribution that

is second only to the United States; unless, that is, we prefer to watch on our television sets the horror of hundreds of thousands dying because we, along with other nations, have failed to mount the massive, complex and extraordinary effort necessary to meet the problem of food aid to these impoverished human beings. They, regardless of colour or distance, are our human brothers and sisters under the skin.
As one with some specialized training in economics, I know that this may be very costly for us and may even mean notable changes in our life-style. But again, realistically speaking, do we have any other alternative, whether we call ourselves Christians, Jews or just humanists? If I am right, this should mean that this nation will have to give the highest priority, for at least the next decade and likely longer, to the production of food. The farmers, of course, will have to be guaranteed a just price so that they will not suffer from the surplus-shortage syndrome that they have had to carry in the past. Little wonder that they are cynical if they are asked to go all out. These and many other difficult problems must be solved within Canada and between the nations who in Rome pledged their support.
Our party does not want to take a "holier than thou" attitude, but we sincerely ask this government to take a strong lead in this, one of the most serious problems to face mankind in its history. After all, the United Nations, and especially the Food and Agricultural Organization, has been warning us of the day of reckoning since at least 1963. This country, and others, I repeat, must place the highest priority on food production. We must develop our latent food capacity and stop using prime agricultural land for non-farm uses. Of course, what we all must realize is that in pressing for very increased production, what the economists call the principle of diminishing marginal return on productivity enters into the picture. In everyday words, when you start seeding and planting new lands you increase the cost of production. Every new acre you bring into production will generally tend to increase the marginal and average price.
We must also improve our grain transportation facilities which all the western members of parliament deplored in debating the grain handlers' strike earlier in the session. It goes without saying that all the countries which pledged their commitment at Rome must also help the very poor countries to improve their delivery systems. Some estimates suggest that only 60 per cent of the grain sent to India ever gets inland to the hungry.
Now I want to talk for a few minutes about the food crisis and population growth in these poor countries. The food crisis is, of course, tied to some extent to their rapid population growth: 74 per cent of the world's population already lives in the Asian, African and Latin-American regions where poverty, poor health and malnutrition are widespread. By the year 2,000 these regions will account for between 81 per cent and 84 per cent, whether fertility declines or not. At the same time, the share of the world population living in the comparative luxury of North America and Europe will decrease from 26 per cent to between 16 per cent and 19 per cent.
I am quoting from the International Monetary Fund projection made in December, 1973. The recent population
World Food Crisis
conference in Bucharest, also sponsored by the United Nations, made clear, though, that the problems of these poor countries is not population growth as such. Population is, of course, a factor in development, but so is international economic equity. The opening paragraph of the "Plan of Action" adopted by consensus of the delegates at the Bucharest conference emphasized that-
The basis for an effective solution of population problems is above all socio-economic transformation.
That idea is recurrent in the document. High fertility rates cannot be lowered by the mere provision of family planning information and material, important as that is. Declines in birth rates and family size are associated with development and modernization, as our own history testifies. Population, moreover, is not the critical source of pressure on the earth's resources and environment. It is consumption that matters, whether by large populations of poor countries or by high per person consumption and waste in the rich countries. In this connection I wish to quote from The Scientific American of November, 1974, at page 49:
It is imperative that all countries, and within them all social sectors, should adapt themselves to more rational utilization of natural resources without excess so that some are not deprived of what others waste.
Mr. Speaker, in concluding these remarks I wish to summarize my thoughts by saying that in the short run the very poor countries with starving and near-starving people need our aid, and we should give it as generously and as efficiently as we can. There is, moreover, the question of trade, as well as aid, which the Canadian delegation at Rome-despite what the Secretary of State for External Affairs said-seemed to sidetrack by their filibustering methods. It should be evident to us that these poor countries need access to our markets at stable and decent prices. They also need help from all the better-off countries, in terms of technology and capital.
On the other hand, Canada, the United States and other donor countries should not be expected to do the following, and I quote Richard N. Garner, professor of law at Columbia University, the originator of the imaginative notion of a "global survival pact" who is referring to the United States but the same sentiment would hold for Canada:
-be willing to give endless amounts of food to an Indian government that cuts its family planning budget, mismanages food production and distribution and invests scarce resources in the testing of nuclear devices.
That quotation is from the New York Times of November 11, 1974, at page 1. In conclusion, I wish to speak on leadership and generosity. Surely we can all agree that the impoverished nations must in the long run feed themselves and must learn to control their population through family planning that does not seem to them to be destroying their dignity or smacking of an imperialistic and racial plot on our part.
It should now be obvious to all of us that it is very difficult to initiate the practice of birth control in a country in which there is little social and economic progress. Surely it behooves Canada and the other "fat cats" of this world to go an extra mile in helping them with very

November 15, 1974
World Food Crisis
generous aid in the short run. This will mean, if millions are not to starve over the next decade, that we and the other donor countries will have put together something much more extensive, in food terms, than a Marshall Plan. I submit that this is a frightening and complex challenge, but only then will we have time to witness new agricultural developments in these poor countries and the hope of adequate population control. I think that the Canadian people will show the depth of their generosity as never before, if they are given leadership on this acute problem of our human family. I say this, coming as I do from an area of Canada where poverty and near-poverty, in Canadian terms, is not unknown to us.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE LEADERSHIP IN SOLVING WORLD FOOD CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on the motion proposed by the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Hogan), I am pleased to have the opportunity again to take part in a debate on a major international crisis being faced in the year 1974. I am grateful that the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond has presented this motion, and for the opportunity to speak again at length on this subject.
Hon. members may recall that on October 21 of this session of parliament I presented a private member's resolution with respect to the establishment of a world food authority. This gave hon. members a brief opportunity to consider the importance and dimensions of the present world food crisis. I think that of immediate concern to all hon. members, and surely to most Canadians, is the question: is there indeed a food crisis? Indeed, we have been inundated in the past few years with a variety of international crises. We have heard of the monetary crisis, the ecological or environmental crisis, the energy crisis, the population crisis and, more recently via the news media, we have heard of the food crisis.
I suppose it is part of the expression of the world in which we live that all of these crises in their turn-and they have considerable dimension-are not confined either within a national boundary or within a regional territory. In a very real sense, they have worldwide dimensions. I suppose we are faced with the situation that one of the problems in dealing with monetary, energy, ecological and population questions is that we have not yet evolved the kind of institutions which can satisfactorily deal with these problems. But I believe it can be said, without fear, of contradiction, that the basic necessity of food for human sustenance and survival is so elemental that no subject could take precedence over it.
We have been told repeatedly and increasingly that food shortages in parts of Africa and Asia and in other localized parts of the world are so acute as to cause severe malnutrition and death, and we realize that we are faced with the greatest crisis of all. It is a grave crisis by any stretch of the imagination, whether or not we talk about it in terms used recently in the New York Times, which indicated that 32 nations are close to starvation. Some of the nations mentioned were Bangladesh, India, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Ethiopia, a whole variety of countries in the northern part of Africa, and specific countries in this hemisphere such as Haita, Honduras, El Salvador and Guyana. These 32 nations which account for hundreds of millions of the world's population have reached such a low-nutrition level that it's becoming increasingly certain that we are on the 
brink, or are already in a situation of the gravest possible nature.
I should like to read the opening paragraph of the preparatory document put forward at the World Food Conference, which perhaps better than any other document presents the situation in which we find ourselves. It reads:
The present world food crisis, originating from a combination of longer term problems and temporary setbacks, suddenly emerged in a pronounced form in 1972. In that year the output of food in the world declined for the first time in more than 20 years.
That indicates to us that we are not dealing with the age-old problem of an insufficient amount of food for specific groups of people related to poor harvests and weather conditions, inadequate trade, or a whole variety of events, some man-made and some that are not within the control of man. We have been told repeatedly in this century that more people in this world go to bed hungry every night than people who go to bed having had sufficient nourishment. That is not the problem to which the World Food Conference in Rome is addressing itself, it is not the problem that we are faced with in 1974, nor the problem that we are discussing today. We are discussing a crisis situation.
It is a well known fact that the year 1970 marded a kind of watershed in world food -production. Until 1970 there was a continual acceleration of food production which was marginally greater than the growth of the world's population. But we know that following 1970 there was a series of new factors which created a growing gap between the world's productivity and the necessity for the vital elements of food. These relate to a number of man-made factors, such as increased prices and cost of production, decreasing revenues for developing countries, more rapid expansion, in certain instances, of population growth, and a disastrous quadrupling of oil prices in a short period of time which subsequently caused shortage of fertilizers and pesticides so badly needed for improved agriculture in the world.
We are faced with, as a result of these factors-I should also include weather and climatic changes- the most serious kind of famine situation in more than 30 nations of the world. It is interesting to think of that situation vis-a-vis our own domestic situation, because 1970 was a peak year for food production in Canada. It was the year in which we had very large domestic production, so large that we had a large food aid program. I think one would have to say that those two went together. The production was so large that we instituted a program to induce farmers to stop producing. Hon. members will recall the now infamous Lower Inventories for Tomorrow program. It seems a shocking program, in light of what we are facing in 1974.
So there is a food crisis. We read the reports published a few months ago by the executive director of the Children's Fund, who warned that the threat of severe malnutrition or even starvation faces 400 million to 500 million children in poorer countries; and hon. members cannot look with equanimity on the fact that large numbers-in the hundreds of millions-of those who are most dependent, women and children, are near starvation. That, of course, is the background of the present World Food Conference
November 15, 1974

taking place in Rome. It is the reason we are being asked to address ourselves to the important question of food aid, changes in the distribution system in the world and in trade, and development programs that are currently locked into a whole range of international relations.
One of the most outstanding happenings, with respect to our country, at this conference is the commitment made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Mac-Eachen) for a million tons of food aid each year for the next three years: it was welcomed in Rome, and I believe it was welcomed in Canada, as an important move toward the alleviation of the immediate food shortage. I think all Canadians support this gesture. However, in the last two or three days there has been a disconcerting approach to the most immediate aspect of the problem, which is, of course, the next 12 months or even the next 8 months because this is the period of most elemental need in a number of countries.
Last Wednesday we were told that our government was prepared to make an announcement, on an immediate basis, of an additional .6 million tons of food aid to countries facing acute food shortages. Yesterday, however, in response to a question from the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) the Secretary of State for External Affairs backtracked. We have heard that the Secretary General of the Food and Agriculture Organization, has lashed out at countries like Canada who are refusing to respond to the most immediate aspect of the problem. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), in Rome, and here at home the Secretary of State for External Affairs, indicated that they are waiting, to put it in the vernacular, to see who else is going to put money on the table before Canada makes its move. In Rome, the Minister of Agriculture apparently expected to see some quid pro quo either from the oil producing nations or other nations who might make a financial contribution that would pay for the aid we are supposed to provide during the current year.
Apart from the commitment we have announced for the next three years, if you look at what has happened in Canadian food aid since 1970-71 you will see it is a sorry story in comparison to world food needs. In 1970-71 we gave 1,271,000 metric tons; in 1971-72, 1,663,000 metric tons; in 1972-73, 782,000 metric tons; in 1973-74, 637,000 metric tons; and the expectation for this year, before the commitment in Rome, was 570,000 metric tons. That is not a record to be proud of in light of the current food situation.
I wonder where the government stands, Mr. Speaker. If we can do nothing else in this debate today, hopefully the Secretary of State for External Affairs or some government spokesman will clarify the government's position with respect to immediate food needs. I think Canadians will be flabbergasted to realize that we have talked magnanimously about contributing a million tons a year for the next three years, and then have completely held off making a contribution when it is needed most, that is, during the next few months. It is monstrous to think that people who are starving can hold out in the expectation of food aid 12 months from now. They will not have the capacity to survive that long.
World Food Crisis
I do not want to speak only about that, Mr. Speaker, although I think it is vital that it be clarified in this debate, but I also want to speak about Canada's general attitude to the World Food Conference. It is an attitude which has depressed me and many members of this House.
I think we have seen very clearly, in this conference, a tremendous vacuum of leadership. Major world nations such as the Soviet Union, the United States and China have, for different or perhaps similar reasons, not been able to provide vital leadership to the conference. In potential, Canada has had a tremendous opportunity. In many ways we were the ideal country to provide leadership to the conference. In a sense, we straddle the fence in that we are one of the more developed nations and yet have many of the characteristics of the underdeveloped world, particularly in the utilization of our natural resources and our energy. We are undoubtedly a major world producer and exporter, as well as a major trading nation.
In view of the absence of leadership by the great nations at this forum, it would have been logical if our two ministers and our official delegation at Rome had worked both at the preparatory conferences and during the past two weeks at the final conference to provide leadership on key questions that have not yet been resolved. But what has our leadership done? We have said, in the first instance, that we are prepared to give food aid for the next three years but we are not prepared to commit ourselves for the immediate future. We have said that discussion on questions of trade and development is not appropriate at this forum and should be discussed under the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade.
In answering questions that I put to the minister on Tuesday and Thursday of this week he seemed to be trying to assure me and other members that if I would only be patient, something beneficial for the developing countries would come out of GATT. If there had been representatives and observers from developing nations in the gallery, I think they would have been shaking their heads sadly to realize that Canada is still committed to an institution which has shown so little responsibility toward freer, fair trade practices in respect of the developing countries. Many years ago GATT was dubbed "the rich man's club". It is basically in response to the failure of GATT to develop appropriate trade relationships with the underdeveloped world that we have had three conferences sponsored by the United Nations Conference on Trade, Aid and Development. Often the shortcomings revealed by the UNCTAD meetings have been the result of the GATT nations only being willing to "talk turkey" in their own forum.
Why cannot this country recognize that we have not yet found an appropriate institutional arrangement through which the underdeveloped countries can develop satisfactory trading relations? The Secretary of State for External Affairs said that he did not think a discussion of these issues at the Rome conference was appropriate, and that we must wait. I find that difficult to understand, Mr. Speaker. The opening speech of the Secretary General of FAO, and the major documents that were prepared for the conference and for the preparatory meetings, offered not only an abundance of evidence of need for restructuring the international economic community, but a series of

November 15, 1974
World Food Crisis
very specific resolutions. The Third Committee, entitled National and International Programs of Action, recommended specific objectives and measures in the area of international trade and adjustment which are relevant to the food problem, including measures toward stabilization and expansion of markets for exports from developing countries.
Our responsibility at Rome was to provide some leadership, some link between the underdeveloped countries of the world, who often focused their presentations on the Group of Seventy-seven, the developed nations and those that are oil producing. Canada is almost unique, in that we have characteristics of an underdeveloped country because we export willy-nilly too many of our unprocessed resources as well as a great deal of energy, and we are heavily integrated with the economy of the United States; and, because of our oil producing capability, we have the opportunity to talk to the OPEC countries. But the Secretary of State for External Affairs has told us that in respect of this conference we will adopt a "wait and see" attitude. That is not international leadership, Mr. Speaker; it is the path of least resistance. Indeed, it is the path of the cowardly lion. I shudder to think that our response to the world food crisis so far has followed that path. Canadians will not hold their heads high in regard to our performance to date on the question of the world food challenge.
I hope it is not too late to take action. There will be conferences, in February of next year, of the United Nations Conference on Trade, Aid and Development- UNCTAD-and following Rome there will be ministerial meetings. I hope that our ministers and their officials will review what has been said in this country. I think there is a substantial and growing body of public opinion that is far ahead of this minister and this government with respect to the problem. I believe Canadians expect much more leadership on this problem than we have received to date. When the minister responds today, I hope he will indicate that he is taking the matter seriously. In the last few months there have been outstanding meetings of nongovernmental agencies in Ottawa and in regional centres. Meetings of agribusiness organizations have indicated they are prepared to make a commitment. The opportunities are immense for the minister to respond to the appetite for leadership, and I hope we shall see the first evidence of this in the debate today.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE LEADERSHIP IN SOLVING WORLD FOOD CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity I have to speak on the motion before us which seeks to blame the government and reads in part as follows:
-condemns the government for its failure, both before and during the World Food Conference in Rome, to provide leadership concerning the food crisis facing many developing nations, and calls on the government to give real leadership on this most acute problem of our time-
Mr. Speaker, our judgment of the proceedings at the latest World Food Conference in Rome must not be onesided. The first question we ask is what has Canada done until now and what should it have done. We must also ask what have and should have other countries done.

That is why it is said that Canada should give leadership or even take the initiative in those matters. Any ordinary and simple man must not aim at doing a giant's work. Without inferring that Canada has done all it could until now, we may assume that it certainly cannot accomplish as much as more powerful countries, because we must remember that its population is only 22 million people and its doings must be related to its size.
As for the needs of underdeveloped countries, no one will deny it is urgent that producing countries offer them help.
When I examine the whole situation, I can see that the main enemy to this aid that all producing countries should be offering to the population of underdeveloped countries is the profiteer. And there is quite a number of profiteers. Mr. Speaker, whether it is an individual, a cartel, a chief of state or even a nation, whoever wants to can find a way to use this aid to make what is known as big money, money which is the economic blood stream of all nations. I believe that in this as in other things, it is still he who controls finances who is often the cause of the atrocious famines which are devastating certain countries.
Mr. Speaker, Canada should concentrate more on the production side and lend a hand to the food industry, expecially agriculture. If we are really living in a favoured country, rich in produce of all kinds, we must stop going against the grain of nature by preventing production, even going to the length of paying farmers to prevent production with the excuse that we will have too much grain and too much beef. The western producers have been paid to prevent them from producing wheat for fear of having too much the next year. Subsidies were granted to egg producers and they were paid to kill chickens because there were too many eggs. Producers in almost every field in Canada are paid to prevent them from producing while two thirds of the world population is starving to death.
That is the ridiculous situation we are living in, here, in Canada. That is why the government should, in future, grant subsidies to that industry par excellence which is agriculture instead of allowing further slaughterings like those which have just been witnessed in my region as a protest against the government. The government should stop granting subsidies to the tune of $100 million and $200 million to multinational corporations and should rather give them to those who produce so that entire populations might live. That is the only way that Canada will be able to help the underdeveloped countries.
May I say that it is one o'clock, Mr. Speaker.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE LEADERSHIP IN SOLVING WORLD FOOD CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the House took recess, I was saying that if the government is to fulfill those promises they made at the World Food Conference, namely to supply underdeveloped countries with more grain, they should give Canadian producers some incentives. I know that if we want to double our production, the only way to encourage Canadian farmers to do so is to double farm aid, because we have to admit that if we are going to help underdeveloped countries, we shall only be sending them our surpluses. We know that Canada has production surpluses and can produce more provided production is not being stymied, and farmers are enabled to cultivate every tillable land in Canada.
Today, Mr. Speaker, 40 per cent of farm lands in my area are not being used for agricultural purposes. In view of world needs, I think this is a shameful situation. We are just behaving like cowards in respect of two thirds of the starving people of some countries who are awaiting their leaders' decisions.
Canada has provided them with grain and a certain amount of money, but I believe the greatest need of those countries is for technical help. I was just reading part of a statement in which the minister said, I quote:
It is therefore likely that the conference will concentrate on the means of increasing food production in developing countries. The conference will however also deal with the necessity to increase world food safety by improving medias and coordinating storage activities.
I believe the major problem of developing countries today simply lies with technical help. We agree that we have to send them food to help them survive until they are in a position to provide for their own needs by themselves. Not only do we have to feed populations for a few months or a few years, but above all to provide them with the means to ensure their own survival. I think we shall have to work harder in that direction in the next few years.
The minister announced in his report that to fertilize the lands in underdeveloped countries, our nation should provide fertilizers and expertise in drainage techniques. I agree with that.
I think that right now those countries are in greater need of water wells than oil wells.
Today all the money is devoted to the oil wells, forgetting the important thing, that is drilling water wells to fertilize the land and allow people to live in a country which can supply them with food and clothing, provided technology enters those countries.
That is what Canada has been doing and can do in the future. I was also wondering what the other industrialized or producing countries were doing. The minister mentioned in his report he would do everything possible as long as the other countries would do their share and also make a commitment, and that is normal. The oil producing countries today do not know what to do with their oil, even in areas of starvation. I suggest the leaders of those countries are criminals and the United Nations should bring them back to order and force them to produce not only oil and arms, but also and more particularly food. I have here an article of La Presse of November 12 entitled "I feel war is close." I quote:
Following the Rabat summit last week Saudi Arabia and a few other oil producing countries undertook to supply annually $1 billion to Syria and Egypt, $300 million to Jordan and $50 million to the PLO for
World Food Crisis
the purchase of arms. That led an observer (cf Times ll-XI-74) to say: "If the United States try to do as much for Israel, their balance of payments will remain in the red forever".
According to Mr. Arafat, the Pentagon intends to do as much for Israel and is currently making haste to deliver huge quantities of arms to them. Why so much money? Why so many arms? If eggs are broken it must be because there is an omelet in the offing.
Such articles, Mr. Speaker, make serious nations shiver. We all are aware of the feeding needs of some people and a war is being prepared with billions of dollars.
The nations which still believe in peace and justice in the world should rise and protest against these things. One will say that they are oil producing countries. If we wanted to use oil today for the sustenance of people, we could do fine things. I read in the Courrier de Vlnde in connection with the struggle against starvation:
Oil proteins should be sold on the market for feed grain, beginning in 1970. A synthetic meat is being developed in the United State from soya beans as well as synthetic milk for human consumption. The congress of the British Veterinary Association is discussing what is called the new era of food.
Mr. Speaker, I believe it would be much more profitable for those countries to get back into this new era of food and to stop playing war, because that is a very dangerous game.
Mr. Speaker, when we look at the other countries, we wonder what they have done with the aid that Canada has given them. Every one knows what has happened in Ethiopia where Canadian gifts have been used by financiers and members of government to line their own pockets.
As for Pakistan, Bangladesh and all those other countries, Canada has taken its responsibilities. The authorities of those countries also have great responsibilities.
I always think of India when it is suggested we send meat to those countries when the people of India still have beef walking around in city streets.
