subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE LEADERSHIP IN SOLVING WORLD FOOD CRISIS
speechtext:
Sacred cows!
Well, I, for one, think that the population should eat those sacred cows instead of letting them walk around in their cities.
I think that world organisations should warn those countries, help them technically and also give them the means to feed their populations.
Mr. Speaker, it is easy to see that in all countries, the governments are sacrificing production to improve their finances and the position of their financial backers.
As I said before, the greatest enemy of all is still financial interests. There will always be people who will think of their financial interests before thinking of saving human lives. While two thirds of the world population are starving to death, those who are holding the purse strings are playing games. The international fat-cat financiers, although they are protected by governments, know that it cannot last. That is why they are looking for an opportunity to provoke a world war to serve their financial interests once again with a deluge of human blood. That is the present situation!

November 15, 1974
World. Food Crisis
Mr. Speaker, some people say:"It's no use reasoning with a hungry man". The underdeveloped countries are ready to do anything to get a meal a day.
Mr. Speaker, my time is almost gone. In conclusion, I hope that the producing countries will awaken and become aware of the situation in the underdeveloped countries and provide them with assistance.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE LEADERSHIP IN SOLVING WORLD FOOD CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to particularly congratulate the mover of today's motion for a statement that set a very good level of debate in this Chamber. I listened to him with a great deal of attention, and there was very little in his speech-a very serious, but moderate speech-with which hon. members of this House could disagree. I think the second speaker for the official opposition, and the hon. member who followed him, also set the tone for this debate concerning a problem we all recognize as being most serious.
On this side of the House we often wonder what the opposition will choose as its subject to present against the government. I think it would have been equally in order for the opposition to have chosen a motion dealing with inflation; they could have talked at some length about the increasing cost of food production and the need for a subsidy on bread to keep the price within the limits of the people of Canada. Their motion could have called attention to the problems of agriculture, and they could have said that the government should do more to stabilize prices to consumers in Canada. That would have been a good and realistic case requiring an answer.
The case of our international responsibility has also been put-that Canada should take the lead in pledging more food to other countries of the world, especially those which have been described in such startling terms as facing famine in our generation. There is no question that the case is good, and convincing. The responsibility of the government is to balance priorities-priorities on the domestic front and on the international front-to meet the total program that is to be presented.
The hon. member for Egmont (Mr. MacDonald) asked a rhetorical question, "Is there a crisis of food production?" Of course, he was very well able to document the fact that there is a crisis. I did not hear him, in the course of this debate-and I regret that I did not hear his previous statement on a private member's motion-amplify his reference to climatological changes which are taking place. This is a subject that has disturbed me and, I am sure, other members of this House. Those of us who have read the works of Professor Reid Bryson, director of the Institute of Environmental Studies at the University of Wisconsin, would have very grave reason to be concerned if just a small fraction of what he is predicting is true.
I should like to call the attention of hon. members to an article that appeared in Science on May 17 of this year, volume 184, No. 4138. It is called "The Perspective of Climatic Change," by Professor Reid Bryson. It is written in fairly technical terms and is a paper presented to the American Association for the Advancement of Science. It is not the kind of article which the average reader would be able to digest in terms of the technical discussion, the

data, charts and evidence. A much more popular version appeared in Fortune magazine in February of this year, by Mr. Tom Alexander. It is entitled "Ominous Changes in the World's Weather". I know there have been prophets of doom from the day of Thomas Robert Malthus, and there have been grave predictions about what is happening in relation to problems of food supply; but many of us have learned that these prophesies of gloom have been grossly exaggerated.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE LEADERSHIP IN SOLVING WORLD FOOD CRISIS
speechtext: It started with Adam and Eve.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE LEADERSHIP IN SOLVING WORLD FOOD CRISIS
speechtext:
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) suggests that perhaps these prophe-sis started in the days of Adam and Eve. I do not think we can dismiss the evidence lightly, and we have an obligation to look upon it. In quoting Bryson's findings, he suggests that we have always assumed in the past that changes in climate are a matter of geological record; they are in the deep and distant past and we do not have to take them very seriously. But Professor Bryson and his institute have, over a period of several decades, carried out very careful studies on changes in the climate in Iceland, careful probes of Greenland's ice-caps, and they have tried to assess over a long period what has happened to our climate.
If there is anything that will send shivers up your spine, it is the reading of some of their predictions. They say that for nearly half of the current century mankind was apparently blessed with the most benign climate of any period in at least 1,000 years. During this kindly era the human population more than doubled, and now there is good reason to believe that the world's climate is reverting rapidly to its less beneficent form. I know that somebody will say at this point, "We have heard that story before," but I suggest there is an obligation to look at the evidence-and the evidence is startling. One of the scholars associated with the team which was considering the longterm trends said:
One of climatology's more surprising recent conclusions, derived from investigations of sea-floor sediments, is that for at least the past 700,000 years, global mean temperatures have been as high as they are now only about 5 per cent of the time.
Then it is said:
-sometimes transistions from one major temperature regime to another have taken place with astounding rapidity, often within a century or so.
Bryson attempts something that many scientists say is still unproved; that is, to provide a global hypothesis of climatic change. I am not competent to do justice to it, but the essence of the forecast is that something is happening around the polar ice-cap which is disturbing wind patterns .on the surface of the globe. He refers to changes in the monsoon in northern India and to patterns in southern France and the northern deserts of the Sahara. He relates this to areas in which droughts are occurring where they did not occur before, and where floods are occurring where they did not occur before. He puts the thesis to us that we are indeed facing a major diminution in food supply areas of the world. If a fraction of what he says is true, the consequences are most serious. He predicts, for example, that the monsoon will not return to northern India in the foreseeable future. Such a prediction would have incalcu-
November 15, 1974

lable consequences to large numbers of people in all parts of the world, should it prove to be true or should it prove to be true for a few years only. There is a crisis. We all accept that. I simply call attention to these two articles because I have not heard reference to them, and the evidence presented is not of a nature that we can lightly or quickly brush aside.
The problems of world food production have been outlined by other hon. members. I have a brother who has spent most of his lifetime studying this matter. He is a professor of food technology in a United States institute. I can barely discuss nor can I read his articles and understand them. But in the course of fishing expeditions in the summer, when we get together, he has said that we should consider what is happening to a number of food exporting nations in the world, particularly those that export proteins. For example, Argentina has ceased to be a food exporter in recent years. What has happened there can only be construed as a tragedy. It cannot be construed by many people who know the field as anything but mismanagement of the food resources of that country.
The failure of the Soviet bloc to develop the agricultural technology which would permit it to take its place among the food exporting nations of the world is a tragedy of our times. The potential food producing areas within the political domination of that bloc are equivalent to those of North America. It is to the North American economy that the world is looking for leadership and for supplies of food. I do not think we in Canada should take a narrow, parochial view of the question of the supply of food on this continent. It is easy to say there are certain techniques in North America, and in so doing we may be accused of being continentalists. Every speaker mentions Canadian food production and agriculture as though this existed on its own without reference to patterns of food development on this continent.
I am proud, as I am sure all hon. members are, of the target pledged by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) when speaking on behalf of Canada at the World Food Conference. Members participating in this debate rightfully have said we should be able to do more. The emphasis clearly is on leadership. We accept that. I do not think anyone in this House would dispute it. We must recognize that there is a very close and intimate association, not only in respect of technology and the means of producing food but also the problems the world faces on a broader front, including the crisis in respect of energy and the crisis in respect of the balance of payments, which is a very serious question; it has caused dislocations in western Europe in countries such as Italy and the United Kingdom.
The spokesman for Canada at the World Food Council- the minister-said, very properly, that it is a matter of long-term, collective planning. We are prepared to accept more than our proportionate share of responsibility because we have the resources and the food capacity; we accept the responsibility because of these facts. We have the responsibility of making sure that our agricultural industry does not follow the lead of countries such as Argentina and others where there has been waste. We must continue to take our place with other food exporting
World. Food Crisis
nations of the world. However, I am sure we would be deluding everybody if we were to suggest that a permanent solution of the world's food problems can be found on the basis of the continuous support of large exporters of food to other areas dependent, as they are, in the short term.
I was particularly interested in the reference by opposition spokesmen to world population problems. The hon. member who introduced the subject was careful and I found myself in substantial agreement with everything he said. But he did make one remark which gave me a little concern. I think I know what he intended. He said that the problem is not population but, rather, consumption so far as large areas of the world are concerned. He said Canada should give the lead by consuming less and exporting more.
I think that is a fair statement of his position. Few of us could disagree with that. However, as a matter of practical politics and a balance of priorities which the government must face, I think we must say there is a very serious problem of population in many areas of the world. It is not just a matter of our consuming less. It was a matter of regret to me to read in the record of the world population conference at Bucharest of the failure by large sections of the world and many countries to accept the responsibility that they clearly must accept in our time. The hon. member who introduced the motion said social and economic development and population policies must go hand and hand. We agree, but these must both progress. There is no way in which the planet can continue to support the population being generated in some parts of the world without the most profound and distressing social consequences for millions and millions of people.
Recently I had the opportunity to visit the General Assembly of the United Nations, where I looked at the population commission forecasts. I believe the member who introduced the motion said that 80 per cent or 84 per cent of the really seriously underprivileged people of the world will be found in the Asiatic regions by the year 2000. I have seen forecasts that are even more shocking. Projections must be made on the assumption of increases in population in our country in our time. We have come very close to something like zero population growth in respect of those who are residents of Canada.
I hope we will always provide a haven for those who suffer from problems of persecution in other countries of the world. We have been a country which has welcomed people from other parts of the world and I am sure we will continue to do so, but I think most of us who have given thought to this matter are beginning to say, and some of my colleagues on this side of the House have said, that the world must relate certain things. It must think in terms of its numbers. It must think in terms of policies which relate to those numbers. It must think in terms of its food supply and must adopt-and the difficulties technologically and economically are immense-social and cultural measures which will lead us to a more rational development of our food supply. The world must plan, not only the use of this food technology but also its energy resources in such a way that there is not serious disruption in respect of other nations attempting to pursue the same goal.

November 15, 1974
World Food Crisis
I believe we can do more and I am sure we will do more: I am sure Canada will do more in the short-term and in the long-term. I am sure we will maintain an efficient agricultural industry which will be one of the finest examples to offer the rest of the world.
I am sure that in the councils of the nations of the world we will continue to call attention to the many fronts on which progress must be made before the spectre of hunger can be averted in our generation. It was the historian Toynbee, a very well read scholar, who said that the tragedy of the twentieth century was that it had the potential and technology to overcome the ancient scourges of illness, famine and lack of shelter, but it could not find the means to apply them.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE LEADERSHIP IN SOLVING WORLD FOOD CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion before us today condemns the government for its failure to provide leadership in the food crisis facing us and asks the government to adopt a trade policy favourable to the future development of countries which are in distress. I am pleased to take part in this debate because I represent one of the great sunshine, food producing areas in Canada, namely, southwestern Saskatchewan. There is growing, worldwide respect for agriculture, and this is as it should be. In Canada we can produce enough food for 60 million people if we go full-out in respect of agriculture. However, in India alone there was an increase in population in the last four years of 70 million people.
We are all aware of the World Food Conference which just ended in Rome. I am sorry to note there were not more firm decisions taken. But now the major grain traders of the world have put off making a decision until they meet in London, England, on November 29 after the regular International Wheat Council meeting. It appears that the immediate need will be for between 185 million and 200 million bushels of wheat in the next 12 months. Canada will be giving away in the next 12 months almost 50 million bushels of wheat. So it is obvious that priority must be given to the agricultural industry and, most important of all, to the producers themselves.
As I said earlier, Canada's food contribution will be mainly in wheat, so I would like to say a few words about this grain. Canada is the largest exporter of high quality bread wheat in the world. Our American friends export more bushels, but it is mainly of the soft, winter variety which is not so well suited to bread-making. Wheat has been connected with the development of man as far back as we can go. A grain of wheat by itself is a small thing, and man by himself is also a small thing. Yet this tiny seed of the grass family changed man's world because, with wheat and bread, he moved out of the cave and was able to control his environment-not be controlled by it. Wheat gave him an everyday food from a grain he could store and plant in a field where he wanted it to grow. Then man went on to live in villages, develop a language and establish laws.
Some men hunted and others planted. With wheat in his hand, man literally walked out of the Stone Age. He went on to build cities and then civilizations. Wheat has a trait denied all other grains. The Egyptians discovered that

yeast made wheat dough rise, and this is how they produced bread. The value of wheat was well known in bygone days. In the days when Rome ruled the world, each legionnaire carried a ration of wheat on his back. Wheat was so greatly revered in China that the emperor made the first planting every season. "Bread" was the loudest cry in the French revolution, and Napoleon's generals wept when they discovered that the Russians had burned the wheat fields which lay ahead. Our young visitors in the gallery today will know that war was never started until the harvest was ripe.
I could go on and on, but with all the progress that our grain industry has made, it must be realized that it still starts from a tiny seed in a wheat field. It knows no race, no creed, no colour, no nationality and no politics. However, in Canada we have never been able to separate wheat from politics. I should like to quote the following words from a radio report of the largest grain handling organization in Canada, the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool:
Recent federal government action in Canada-and in some cases lack of it-came under heavy fire November 12, from E. K. Turner, president of Saskatchewan Wheat Pool.
Speaking at the annual meeting, Mr. Turner said:
"I would like to see the federal budget introduce measures designed to curb inflation, but the interests and priorities of the government appear to lie in other direction."
The president also said pool members, as farmers and operators of a business, "must express our concern about the heavy-handed interference of the federal government".
Mr. Turner is further quoted as saying:
"Now we are finding that, increasingly, marketing decisions are being made by politicians and civil servants. Decisions relative to our own operations are being imposed from outside. Farmers' choices are being limited by government decree".
Those are strong words, but unfortunately they are true. Mr. Ira K. Mumford, general manager of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool, in reviewing problems of concern to farm people said the following at the same meeting:
"Excessive public debate about the future grain handling and transportation system and new government grain programs are confusing and unsettling to say the least".
This government seems determined to keep our agricultural industry in a state of turmoil and confusion. Nobody seems to know where we are going. Over the past decade we have been subject to an ideological and political war in Canada over the future of this basic agricultural industry. On the one hand we heard economists conclude from their statistics and projections that agriculture was a poor yield investment and the agricultural industry a dispensable social problem. Quite dispassionately, and on what appeared to them to be perfectly logical economic grounds, they declared both the agricultural community and our wheat industry to be expendable. We know now that that was wrong.
On the other hand, just as scientific and dispassionate in their approach and their arguments were the nutritionists who looked mainly at projected increases in world food needs, and the demographers who studied the frightening rate of increase in the world's population. So on one hand we had a group of experts telling Canada, in effect, to get out of agriculture and into some other, more profitable sphere of industrial output, to cut our heavy social over-
November 15, 1974

head by guiding people off the farms and into urban centres of industry, and on the other hand we had another group of experts saying, "Make agriculture more technology-oriented, more productive, more widespread, more active, not only in the national interest but in the interest of all mankind." We know now that the latter approach is the correct one, but it took us a long time to get there.
We must make sure what this is all about because, after all, it is people and not institutions and systems that we should be worrying about. The problem in the world today is the widening gap between the demand for food and its production, especially in the developing world. The question is, how did we arrive at this situation, dnd for what reasons, because all the developing countries are predominantly agricultural and yet find they cannot produce to feed themselves? This, then, is the key question.
I notice that in the motion before us the government is being urged to adopt a trade policy favourable to the future development of these countries. I think the answer has its roots in the past 25 years or so in the western world when we stressed massive development and planning. Most of the money and effort in agriculture has been going into capital investment projects for cash crops for export, so as to earn foreign exchange to pay for imports. In the developing countries most of the staple foods are grown by peasants who were neglected in most of the aid and economic development plans. So the ineviatble happened: when you neglect the staple food producer, food production will stagnate and population and costs rise. Sooner or later the gap causes problems.
That is where we are now, and none of us can escape the worldwide consequences. Hundreds of millions of peasants were drawn into the world's market economy as consumers, not as producers. They were taught to want education, to become doctors and engineers, to want transistor radios, king sized cigarettes and Coca-Cola. Mr. Speaker, we should forget about trying to build up a middle-class hooked on our western standards. These people were not taught how to grow and produce more goods to pay for all the things they had learned to want, nor to feed all the extra mouths better health had brought them.
It is interesting that last night the Canadian Wheat Board stated that of the grain we give to Asian countries, about 20 per cent is spoiled by rodents and infestation. That means that if Canada is going to give up to 50 million bushels of grain per year, at least 7 or 8 million bushels will be spoiled. I assure that grain is worth about $7 per bushel laid down in those countries, which means that about $50 million of the taxpayers' money would be wasted every year. Surely there is an opportunity for the government to do something to correct this situation.
These are several attitudes toward foreign aid, Mr. Speaker. The cynical opinion, of course, is that it is an instrument of international exploitation on a grand scale. Another view is that the rich countries were genuinely committed to providing money to promote development in the rest of the world. We all like to think that the poor countries will seize the opportunities and resources offered and that there will be a dramatic eradication of
World Food Crisis
poverty, ignorance and disease in those countries. Surely the truth must be somewhere in between. The rich countries do have interests other than the welfare of far away people, and the governments of the poor countries are as interested in their own political survival as in economic change.
Only now we are beginning to realize the seriousness of the situation which was spelled out so well by the World Food Conference held in Rome. Farmers should not hesitate to speak out, because they have the biggest stake in the agricultural business. Grain policy must emanate from the farm. The misfortune of other people around the world has helped our agricultural industry in Canada, so we can take no credit for policies developed here. Our agricultural industry has survived in spite of the government's action.
A group of farmers, members of the International Federation of Agricultural Producers, attended the World Food Conference in Rome as official observers but as a non-governmental body. They announced that they were very upset at the way the view of producers were being ignored by the conference secretariat. Mr. Charles Munro, the Canadian president of this international federation, said there had been a marked lack of consultation with farming interests when the conference agenda was drawn up. He said that the people who actually produce food have more right than many governments or economists to make decisions.
The question now, Mr. Speaker, is whether the nations of the world will co-operate in this food crisis, or will each nation see its special advantages as a weapon? Canada must re-examine the priorities and practices of her food production. We have tended to pile more and more plans and papers for the solution of food and population crises on the desks of the overworked civil servants of these developing countries. We need more than glib moralizing. I repeat what the hon. member for Egmont (MacDonald) said earlier: there is a growing body of public opinion in this country whose thinking is far ahead of that of this government.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, in the short term, food grain must be rushed to the famine-threatened areas. In the long term, world grain production must increase dramatically. Canada must do her share, starting with some clearcut policies by this government.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE LEADERSHIP IN SOLVING WORLD FOOD CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have the opportunity to join in the debate on this important topic. The hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Hogan) has done us all a service by raising the matter for discussion. While I do not agree with his criticism of Canada's performance to date, I certainly support his concern that Canada's contribution be as effective as possible.
Canadians have always been deeply concerned with their moral and social responsibilities as world citizens, and have tried to give expression to that concern in ways that are practical, effective and acceptable to the other countries involved.
Our approaches to international aid have involved giving both immediate, practical aid and the kind of assistance toward long term planning that allows develop-

November 15, 1974
World Food Crisis
ing nations to improve their capability to handle their domestic food production, and so on.
One good example of this kind of broad approach is our assistance to the six countries of Africa's droughtstricken Sahel region following a study by CIDA. In addition to supplying food and transport trucks, our projects were aimed at solving problems in agriculture, transportation, food storage, stock raising, reforestation and the provision of fresh water to villages and grazing areas. The project to provide 85 wells in 85 villages in one region of Niger was tied in with existing development plans. I think this kind of careful long term planning may be one of our strengths.
The world food conference had a twofold aim, Mr. Speaker. The immediate problem was to deal with depleted world grain stocks, high prices for food grains, the shortage of fertilizers and so on, and next, to deal with the problems in the longer term.
Canada's response to the need for immediate assistance was prompt. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) announced a gift of one million tons of food grains annually for each of the next three years, and requested other nations to follow this example. A prompt, generous and direct gift of food is a necessary short term solution or answer to an emergency situation; the longer term answer is surely to help nations produce their own food. The $1 Vi million we granted to Bangladesh to help buy new crop seeds for fall planting, for farmers whose properties had been flooded, was useful. It would have been less useful had it not been made in relation to an ongoing program of Canadian food aid and a knowledge of local conditions, which made it possible to introduce new kinds of winter crops to areas normally left unplanted during the dry season.
I understand that Canada's aid program in 1974 will be about $733 million, including $100 million for food aid and fertilizer. I believe we have attempted to strike a responsible balance between direct aid and helping people to help themselves. Helping people to improve their competence will become increasingly important in the future. I believe this is a role particularly well suited to Canada. We are trusted by the developing nations because we are not a major power and because our commitment to human betterment is well known. Individual Canadians are usually well suited to this role. Anyone who observes this House will of course see that we are very modest and conciliatory people.
Seriously, I think our young people overseas with CUSO, and some of our retired people who have gone to lend their expertise in various projects have been very useful. They have shown their ability to accommodate to local conditions, a respect for local knowledge, and a capacity and willingness to work patiently with a situation rather than impose an alien technology. It has been said that we are going to be asked in the future to lend our best people for projects overseas. I would like to think that perhaps our greatest contribution in the future may be made by giving people expertise rather than direct aid, important though that may be.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE LEADERSHIP IN SOLVING WORLD FOOD CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I commend the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Hogan) for reminding us, if indeed we needed reminding, that one of the most vital of the many conferences that seem to proliferate in the world these days is taking place in Rome.
We have a term of reference that I think is somewhat apt, by a great poet, Auden, who said wisely "When truly brothers, men don't sing in unison but in harmony." I hope very much that the results of this debate will mean just that. Although there may be political differences, the harmony that can come from such a debate is a will on the part of the government to do what other speakers have said is uniquely in the capacity of this country to do, that is, to provide the type of leadership the world must have if people are not to starve.
In another context I heard a reference to what must be one of the most cynical phrases of the age, that is, that the world is suffering from compassion fatigue. If I knew more about the method man uses to communicate with others, perhaps I could share with the House some observations about this. Some day it might be useful to have a debate on the fact that we are now almost shock proof. Statistics of death, destruction and famine come to us at such momentum that we somehow turn them off, Mr. Speaker. I am sure that is not deliberate. If it is, it is the end of civility as we know it.
The other what I think must be an obscene part of contemporary man is that although mankind is quite able to find cash for armament, we do not seem to have evolved any system of finding cash for those who hunger.
We have had a fairly careful analysis by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) and others of the immediate problem. The immediate problem is the real hunger of south-east Asia and the south Sahara region of Africa which, we understand, face a grain shortage of between seven and 11 million tons. We have also had the statistic that 15 per cent of the production of fertilizer in the United States is devoted to what might be called a trivial use, that is, for lawns, gardens and golf clubs. If that could be diverted to assist in growing crops a real impact could be made in countries where there is need.
We realize that those who have the most surely have the greatest obligation to sacrifice the most. Perhaps that is a trite observation, but no one taking part in this debate thinks that any solution can be found without personal sacrifice and also sacrifice by our government and the governments of the other developed countries.
My colleague, the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. Hamilton), reminded us of another immorality of the last decade. That was a program known as LIFT. The interesting point is that two privy counsellors mentioned the immorality of LIFT, one a former Minister of Agriculture, the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton), and the other, the present Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan).
In his former capacity the Minister of Agriculture-and I quote from a book "Hard to Swallow" by Walter Stewart-spoke or wrote to several members of the federal cabinet from his position in the back benches warning the government of the results of that wrong-headed policy.
November 15, 1974

The minister is deserving of a great deal of honour for his foresight.
In a debate about hunger we have to remember that wrong-headed policy. There is no point in sloughing it off and saying it did not happen. It was a deliberate policy of the government, which undoubtedly directly affected the lives of a great many of our brothers and sisters in the world.
I wish to comment on something rather unique that has been happening in Rome. Most of those involved perhaps would not wish me to mention them by name, but I want to mention a very helpful combination of the Canadian Council of Churches and the CCIC. They have provided a sort of latter day truth squad for the benefit of all members of this House.
This GATT-FLY organization went to the UNCTAD Three Conference in Santiago. However, at that time it had not developed a means of communicating quickly with members of parliament or, for that matter, ministers. This time the GATT-FLY group were supported by technical people who were the match of the public servants.
I have no reason to condemn the dedicated public servants who serve the government. The problem is that many of us do not have enough access to those public servants. However, access was provided by GATT-FLY. I commend them for their important addition to our knowledge of this subject. They have informed us on a daily basis of what the government of Canada is up to-they have urged us to commend when commendation is due, and they have urged us to get more information when more information was due us.
As a matter of fact, within the past few minutes they have been in touch with us about a rather negative decision made in the third committee in Rome. That went on just as this debate went on. It was, really, a retreat on the part of the developed nations, including Canada, in the face of the draft resolution presented by Mexico. Many of the requests contained therein were turned down by Canada and other developed countries. As a matter of fact, there was almost no reference to terms of trade.
The reference to just prices for exports in relation to imports was deleted. Deleted, too, was the reference to refunding customs duties, as was the specific reference to the maintenance of reserve stocks of basic cereals with the aim of improving market stability. Most of the references to UNCTAD were deleted, while GATT was played up-

That telegram was sent as a result of unanimous agreement reached by a broad cross-section of this country.
It was our feeling that the government is to be commended for the initiative shown in the short term but that, having earned this commendation, the government cannot be allowed to hive off its responsibilities on a world food board, for instance. We also asked for long term solutions to be integrated into measures for economic reform, perhaps by the United Nations. Obviously, we lost that wicket because now we see what happened to the resolution proposed by Mexico. The result leaves much to be desired.
I suppose we all have various ways of manifesting our love for our country. I think it is right that each of us has an individual way of evoking what Canada means to us. The test I have for this country-and I hope many of my colleagues share this feeling-is how we treat our fellow men, or our fellow humans, to put it in the contemporary vernacular. Mr. Speaker, there has not yet come from the Rome Conference, and I am sorry to say this, any sign that Canada is able to meet the test of treating our fellow humans with civility and compassion. This, I regret very much.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE LEADERSHIP IN SOLVING WORLD FOOD CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my intervention in the debate following that of the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Hogan) and the hon. member for Egmont (Mr. MacDonald) will make it rather ecumenical now. Perhaps, though it was not designed to be that way, it does have its own kind of symbolism, because what we are really talking about is not so much an agricultural, or even a food problem, supposed to be the substance of the debate today, but rather, a moral issue. In many ways it is the central moral issue of our times. The question is: to what extent are we as a people, as individuals, as a nation, prepared to move away from our own self-centredness and start thinking of others?
I was interested listening to the remarks made by the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Francis). I always enjoy his contributions, and I would like to reply to some of the things he said in the serious way in which everyone is discussing these serious problems today. On the question of government priorities the hon. member pointed out, and it is true, that government has all kinds of priorities in the same way that people have all kinds of priorities. There is inflation that they are worried about; there are priorities with regard to employment. But how do those priorities really compare with the priorities being faced by millions of people in the world who are nearing starvation?

November 15, 1974
World Food Crisis
In our society we have become accustomed to taking each other apart about things which, at best, are merely increments to our already high standard or living. When you place the problems we face against those faced by much of the rest of the world, certainly our difficulties pale by comparison. Can there really be any question of juggling priorities when so much of the world is facing death from starvation? Is it not time we realized that there is one central priority-our responsibility to other human beings? If that means there must be some belt-tightening in this country, if that means we have to slow down somewhat the rise in our standard of living, surely this is what we as human beings, we as a nation, must be prepared to accept.
There has been a reference to Toynbee, a writer many of us have read, and his contention that though it is within our power to put an end to hunger and many of the diseases which afflict mankind, we have yet to devise an effective technique to achieve these ends. The great failure of modern society has been its failure to find this technique. Toynbee's solution is a return to religion. But if you want to take it in a broader sense, what Toynbee is really suggesting is a return to morality. Now, for many, religion has lost its hold, but surely the basis of religion, the idea of morality, has not lost its hold and should not lose its hold on the western world.
It is true we can do all these things mentioned by Toynbee, but we have to see this as a moral issue in order to meet the challenge we face. The hon. member for Ottawa West said that we had to plan the use of the resources of the world. We do not even plan the use of our own resources in this country, let alone plan the use of the resources of the world. We must make a start on planning within this country, particularly in the agricultural field.
Traditionally when we considered the problems of agriculture and food supply it was always in this kind of setting: either we have viewed them from the viewpoint of the consumer-how we can keep food prices down, or how we subsidize consumers; or we have viewed them from the point of view of the producer-will over production affect prices, will the producer be disadvantaged, what is the trade-off between the consumer and the producer?
It seems to me that a third element has now entered into this debate. We can no longer look at agriculture exclusively from the viewpoint of the price paid to the producers by the consumers. We have to look at it from the viewpoint of all out production in order to prevent a great many of the people of the world from starving. This is the kind of approach we should now take to agriculture. This is the kind of planning we must do in our own country before suggesting that the world should also plan.
When you look at agriculture in those terms, you get an entirely different perspective. I think we have made a decent gesture at the food conference in offering one million tons of grain a year. That is a start. But even if we give more-and I think we should give more-and start to plan now to bring more land under cultivation, and to employ our technology better, there are many people who say that we are too late, that regardless of what action we

take now the problem is so severe we will be unable to produce sufficient food to head off starvation.
Knowing that there is a distinct possibility that we may well be too late and that starvation will occur despite our best efforts, we are faced with a situation where we must do everything we possibly can, not because we alone can stave off starvation, not because we can eliminate it entirely, but because we have to live with ourselves and to ask ourselves what we did to alleviate the situation confronting humanity. And we must come up with an answer that does not offend against humanity.
In formulating a new agricultural policy we must think in terms of meeting the world's needs. I do not know that our traditional methods of farm or consumer subsidies are going to be appropriate. It seems to me we cannot ask the farmers to bear the cost of our generosity toward humanity. The farmer is, of course, a member of society and will bear his share, but this is a cost that has to be borne by all members of society, not one particular group.
We must guarantee to the farmer an orderly marketing system for his products, rather than let the farmer produce products he cannot sell and thus go into bankruptcy. Today there is a market for food, but there are not many people who can afford to pay the market price.
At the same time there must also be a willingness on the part of society to reduce consumption. The other day I introduced a private member's bill which would amend the Criminal Code to make the destruction of food a criminal offence. Many people have asked me where you stop. The bill appeared to be pointing at the farmer. I was not pointing at the farmer but to society in general. I was pointing to the fact that in a world where people are dying of starvation it is wrong to destroy food. It is wrong to destroy food in order to increase one's own benefit. That was the principle I was trying to establish.
People came to me and asked me what I was going to do to a man who orderd a huge dinner that he could not possibly eat, and then sent it back because the food did not have the right sauce on it. I was asked whether my bill would send that man to jail for destroying food. It is patently impossible either to send that man to jail or to send anybody else to jail in such a situation, but it is not impossible for society to say that such a man is committing a wrong. The fact that he can afford to send back his steak does not give him the right to destroy that food, food that would sustain life somewhere in the world.
This is one of the issues society has to face, and it is one of the lessons we must teach ourselves. In the course of debates on this subject people hesitantly ask, perhaps with the best of intentions, whether it is not their own damn fault that these countries are short of food. I do not think any member of parliament would make the point in quite those terms, but that was the implication of what was said. People would say; "These countries have too many children and are not practising birth control. They are ignoring the advice that we give them. They are letting food rot and spoil. There is a lot of corruption in their society, so isn't it their own damn fault?"
No doubt there is fault somewhere, but the point is that we are destroying much of the food that these people need. This is no time to lecture people. We used to do this with
November 15, 1974

our own poor. I can recall some hesitant ventures in this regard when we were talking about elderly people who reached their old age without a pile of money in the bank. It was said that it was their own fault because they did not save their money while they were earning. Or it was said of someone who was ill that he should have been more careful and not had his accident. Or it was said of someone who had more children than somebody else approved of that is was their own damn fault to have so many. Now we no longer point this kind of accusing finger.
We have now reached a level of understanding. We appreciate that when we eliminate some of the disadvantages experienced by these poor people we do not have to lecture them about birth control or about saving money; they respond in their own way.
The underdeveloped countries make the excellent argument that you cannot deal with their social problems by lecturing them; you can only deal with them by finding some way of giving them a sense of security and support. To some people who live in underdeveloped countries, having children is security in their old age, particularly when they know that famine might take some of their children away. To tell these people not to have so many children is to take away what to them is social security. Until we can tell those people that if they get sick, or that when they get old there will be support for them from the western world, we are not going to change the pattern regarding family size.
As much as we talk about what we are going to do for other people, we also talk about what we are going to do for ourselves. I do not really believe that our society is going to sleep well if it knows it has not taken action to prevent human starvation. I do not see how we are going to have a society of affection, respect and love when we narrow this to our own boundaries or our own families. Whatever we do, and it may appear on the surface as a form of generosity, we are really doing it for ourselves as well. We do have an obligation to others and to ourselves to do everything we can in food aid to stave off a disaster that is facing the world.

World Food Crisis

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE LEADERSHIP IN SOLVING WORLD FOOD CRISIS
speechtext:
Apart from the argumentation that may have been produced in the debate the resolution seems intended more to berate the government for its failure to feed the hungry. I do not accept the suggestion that the Canadian government, before the conference, did not pay appropriate attention to the seriousness of this issue. In fact, my predecessor, speaking this past winter before the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence, and again when he addressed the United Nations General Assembly in special session in April, identified the food crisis in the world as being of top priority.
From the first meeting of the preparatory committee of the World Food Conference last February, Canada has been very active and has participated in all of the important preparatory conferences. Our ambassador in Rome has been given special responsibilities in attending the preparatory meetings in order to express Canadian concern and advise the Canadian government as to developments.
A special task force was set up within the government in February to prepare for the conference. The deputy secretary general of the conference was in Ottawa in May for intensive discussions on how to get the best results out of the conference. I attended the final part of the agroindustry meeting in Toronto which took place under the auspices of the World Food Conference, consisting of a wide group of the executive and agro-industry people throughout the world, for the purpose of determining how they could contribute to the results of the World Food Conference.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) held discussions with all the provincial agriculture ministers on this problem in July, and out of that conference came a decision to name two provincial representatives to the World Food Conference as members of the delegation, one of whom is the minister of agriculture for Saskatchewan. I doubt whether he would share the language that is found in this motion as a commentary on the attitude of the Canadian government.
Federal officials have travelled from one end of Canada to the other to brief provincial governments on the issues, and to advise them on how we saw the conference developing. As hon. members know, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and his provincial counterparts discussed the world food situation at the recent conference on inflation, and they agreed on the necessity of close federal-provincial co-operation in ensuring that Canada plays its full role in helping to meet the emergency and the long-term situation.
We did have a good delegation in Rome composed of representatives of the public service, ministers from the provincial governments, members of parliament who attended all delegation meetings and, as hon. members who spoke earlier know, persons from non-governmental organizations.
I did attend the first week of the conference in Rome, and I should like to convey to the House the impressions I formed during my short stay about problems of food and malnutrition in the world. We are all acutely aware of the dimensions of this problem in the world, and of the many difficulties in the way of solving the problem and elimi-

World Food Crisis
nating hunger in the world. If there is any doubt about the difficulties that have been implied and disclosed in the proceedings at the World Food Conference, I am ready to say that the week I spent in Rome has convinced me, beyond any doubt, that the problems are even more acute than we suspected, and I think now demand an unprecedented urgency.
When I left, the debate was still continuing in the plenary session and the committees had just begun their detailed work. But I can say, apart from reporting on the results of the detailed work, which I am unable to do, that a general consensus did emerge at the conference on the urgency of the problem and the necessity of immediate measures to deal with it.
Again on behalf of the Canadian government and the Canadian people, the Canadian statement at the conference outlined the measures Canada intends to adopt to share common endeavours toward a lasting freedom from want for all mankind.
Our position can be summarized in seven points, and I believe they ought to be put on the record in light of the importance of this debate.
First, Canada is prepared to accord a high priority in its assistance program to the agricultural development of countries which are mobilizing their own resources to increase food production. Let there be no doubt about it, Mr. Speaker, that even with the best of goodwill and with the most vigorous efforts on the part of the developed world there is no way by which starvation in the developing countries can be overcome without the acceleration of food production in the developing countries themselves. There is no doubt about that.
Even if we did have food in the developed world in millions of tons in the future there is doubt whether it can be transported or distributed to the needy people in light of projected population increases over the next period of time. The Chinese delegation, speaking at the conference, said, "Do as we have done; feed yourself". In a sense that was good advice, but it certainly was no answer to the critical short-term food shortage in the developing countries.
Second, Canada will do what it can to mitigate shortages of agricultural input in respect of such things as fertilizer, and will see to it that access to these is maintained internationally on an equitable and non-discriminatory basis. Reference has been made to fertilizer. It is an essential input. Earlier this year, before the Rome food conference, we did commit an additional $100 million to food and fertilizer. I think $43 million of that has been spent on providing fertilizer, but we are limited in what we can do because we do not have, for distribution abroad, the nitrogenous fertilizers which are needed in the developing countries.
Reference has been made to potash. Potash is not wanted. Therefore, we are not able to help in that direction. Rather, Canada intends to play its full part in the accelerated programs that we are asking the competent agencies to devise to make a sustained attack on the problem of malnutrition, particularly among children and other vulnerable groups.

It is to be underlined, as one of the saddest pieces of information emerging from the conference that 200 million children and nursing mothers are malnourished at the present time. That problem has not been highlighted very much, but we have said to the United Nations agencies, to UNICEF and others, please take note of this problem of malnutrition and we, as a government and as a country, will be prepared to support your efforts in tangible terms in order to reduce this problem of malnutrition.
Fourth, Canada has committed itself to making available, in each of the next three years, an average of one million tons of foodgrains toward a minimum world target of 10 million tons for food aid purposes. We have also committed ourselves to a significant increase in the non-foodgrain commodities which we allocate to food aid. We have agreed to channel some 20 per cent of our total food aid through multilateral food programs such as the World Food Program. All these were proposals put before the conference by the secretariat. I regret to say that in the first week of the conference relatively few countries made any effort to respond directly to the proposals that had been put before the conference by the Secretary General, the former minister of agriculture from Egypt.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE LEADERSHIP IN SOLVING WORLD FOOD CRISIS
speechtext: Why?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE LEADERSHIP IN SOLVING WORLD FOOD CRISIS
speechtext:
Why? That is a good question. I wish I knew the answer. Very few countries did. I hope to reach what their commitments were and possibly compare them with the Canadian commitment. I agree with hon. members who have said we ought to be generous, forthcoming, and show our humility in Canada, but when we do that in a responsible way let us not denigrate what we have done.
Let us take the responsibility for telling the Canadian people what the Canadian response has been. In respect of the 3 million tons, 1 million each year, in volume terms not in dollar terms, the Secretary General pleaded with the world community at the conference to please commit 10 million tons per year in volume terms, as a minimum for the next three years. We committed one-tenth of that, which is more than our proportional share, in the expectation that that would induce other countries possibly to come forward and increase the total commitment beyond that 10 million tons. That is the benchmark against which we were working-the proposal made by those who prepared for the conference.
Let us not underestimate the financial consequences of that commitment. One million tons of wheat, at at least $200 a ton, each year will cost us at least $200 million. The reason we have asked to make it in dollar terms is to ensure that the wheat goes forward regardless of the possible increase in the price of wheat in the next few years.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE LEADERSHIP IN SOLVING WORLD FOOD CRISIS

November 15, 1974

that had been put before the conference by the Secretary General who had asked all the world to please give, as a minimum, 10 million tons per year for the next three years. We took 10 per cent of that. Surely on any count that is more than proportional to the financial resources of Canada in its position in the world. This was so recognized by the conference itself.
It is reported in the press that the Australian delegates immediately sought instructions from Canberra, from their Prime Minister, to match the Canadian contribution. The Secretary General of the conference publicly stated that the statement made by the Canadian delegation was a turning point in the conference itself.

This newspaper states about the Canadians:
They've come up trumps ...
Canada and Australia put their money on the line yesterday during speeches in the Plenary ...
The Canadian Secretary of State for External Affairs, Mr. Allan J. MacEachen, started the ball rolling in the morning session...
I refer to another editorial comment that was made by the Christian Science Monitor, because it was referred to at the Rome conference by one of the most distinguished columnists. That editorial stated:
Canada is to be commended for its pledge at the World Food Conference to boost its food aid to hungry nations by 20 per cent in the next three years.
In fact, in terms of volume the commitment next year to the world food need is double the commitment we have made this year. The editorial went on to say:
Hopefully, this initiative will meet vigorous response from other nations as well.

Canada has succeeded in making a very favourable impression in spite of the criticism being voiced in the Canadian press at home. The Canadian agricultural minister, Eugene Whelan, has been one of the few ministers of cabinet rank to stay in Rome for the whole fortnight of the conference ... A
World. Food Crisis
group of 32 most seriously affected countries which got together earlier in the week, spoke approvingly of Canadian attitudes.

speechtext: So did we.

speechtext:
I am delighted that the hon. gentleman disassociates himself from the resolution which seems to condemn the government for its performance at the Rome Food Conference.
Canada has endorsed the principle of a voluntary undertaking in world food security, and will become a party to it when the necessary arrangements have been worked out, Mr. Speaker.
Sixth, Canada supports, as it has long suggested, a general freeing of trade in food products and will press this objective and other benefits for the trade of developing countries in the forthcoming multilateral trade negotiations in Geneva.
I am happy to say that despite the charge levelled earlier today that the Canadian delegation was filibustering and that we were not taking a helpful attitude in committee III, today the world conference in committee III has completed its work and reached unanimous agreement on grain measures. It is a reasonable text, and the Canadian delegation has played an active part in reaching this good result which will lay a foundation for the detailed negotiation that will take place in the upcoming discussions at GATT.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE LEADERSHIP IN SOLVING WORLD FOOD CRISIS
speechtext:
Surely the developing countries, which unanimously agreed to this resolution, are in a better position to determine their own interests than is the hon. member for Egmont (Mr. MacDonald).
Finally, I want to conclude the point form presentation of our position by saying that Canada announced its decision to allocate at once $50 million of our development assistance to be used in ways that will make an effective impact on the present critical world food situation.
My hon. friend has asked: what about today, what about the current situation? Of course it is a critical situation. Up to the present we have committed more than 600,000 tons of grain for this year. The problem that has been bothering the people at the conference is the basic one of supply, the determination in the next months about what is available in the world in the way of supplies of grain in order to meet the requirements in the developing countries. We have participated in that exercise to determine what is required.
It is estimated that we have an amount of 1,300,000 tons which could be made available. It is obvious to hon. members that for Canada to finance in this current year, in addition to 600,000 tons, an additional 1,300,000 tons is an enormous commitment ot undertake at this stage. What we have said on this point is that we have already put forward $50 million that can be used for food aid in the current year, and I have been informed-but I would like to check this information further-that we have completed further allocations at the conference, among needy countries at present, from this amount. However, I would like to make sure that that is absolutely right.

November 15, 1974
World Food Crisis
So we are not finished yet, and I hope hon. members opposite will believe that there beats in our souls, as energetically as in theirs, an interest in this problem, and that the love of humanity does not only exist on the other side.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE LEADERSHIP IN SOLVING WORLD FOOD CRISIS
speechtext: Nobody said it did.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE LEADERSHIP IN SOLVING WORLD FOOD CRISIS
speechtext: We demonstrated our intentions, our proposals, in a more concrete way than any other nation in the world. The hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond asked, "But what is the standard?" Perhaps he would accept Sweden as a standard. The NDP has always been applauding the great social system that exists in Sweden. It is a country that has a higher per capita income than Canada, and yet I think that our contribution compares favourably with that country's. Sweden has committed to make available, on call each year, a substantial amount, 75,000 tons of grain.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE LEADERSHIP IN SOLVING WORLD FOOD CRISIS
speechtext: How much grain do they produce?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE LEADERSHIP IN SOLVING WORLD FOOD CRISIS
speechtext:
I would remind the hon. member that you can supply grain or you can finance it. There are two ways to do it. So let him not hedge the situation by that comment. If we go down the list of donors we find Iran, Saudi Arabia, Poland, the European Economic Community, Norway, Austria, and if you compare their creditable showing and ours-and I do not for a moment take anything away from them-Canada has shown leadership.
It is false to say that we have failed to give leadership at the conference. It is true to say that if the leadership provided by Canada had been followed, and its contribution matched by other countries, the conference would be adjourning tomorrow with a much greater message of hope to the starving people of the world then they will be given when it concludes tomorrow evening.
I want to say, as I said to the non-governmental organizations when I met them in Rome that this is only the beginning of the effort, because it is an effort that will engage the attention of mankind probably for the next decade, to feed the starving people of the world.
I regard the problem of hunger as great if not greater than any of the other global problems. I assure the House, particularly any hon. members who may have been uncertain, that the Canadian government is giving leadership and will continue to do so-leadership that might not be applauded by hon. members opposite but which has received plaudits around the world.
