That is what I have in mind, not the NGOs.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE LEADERSHIP IN SOLVING WORLD FOOD CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the World Food Conference in Rome has come and gone; previous to its commencement some 12,000 people per day were dying of starvation. With the conference over, 12,000 people per day will continue to die of starvation. While the government can accept some small pride for its efforts, it is cocooned in a notion that it really did something, that it took some small steps. I have to underline the word small because although the leadership it claims may be apparent to it, the fact of the matter is it did almost nothing to solve the world problem of hunger.
The pre-planning conference committee had three points on its agenda-first, to increase food production in developing countries by at least 35 per cent by 1985; second, to improve distribution to make consumption more equitable and third, to establish food reserves as insurance against crop failures and other disasters. United Nations Secretary General Kurt Waldheim opened the conference by asking for a double onslaught by all countries on world hunger. The fact of the matter is, Mr. Speaker, that our contribution is nowhere near the kind of commitment requested, or the kind of commitment necessary to cope with the problem at hand.
We can note four or five points of criticism of Canada's participation at this conference, Mr. Speaker. First, there is not enough aid; second, there was no argument for an adequate structure for the distribution of aid throughout the world nor the leadership to encourage such structures; third, little was done in terms of helping developing coun-

November 15, 1974

tries to provide for themselves; fourth, little has been done to ask us to change our lifestyle in terms of food consumption; and fifth, there was little or no suggestion that Canada ought to be increasing her present food production.
Let us look at some of the things we have given the developing countries. It would seem we have given them one slice of bread every five days. According to international experts, by 1985 the poor countries of the world will need 85 million tons of grain per year from the developed world. It could well be they would require something in excess of 100 million tons of food or cereal grains per year in less than a decade.
Even if such an amount were available, it could not be moved, Mr. Speaker. One of the things this conference can be criticized for is the lack of planning for the transportation of foodstuff around the world. We should remember how our ports and railroads were fouled up when Russia bought 15 million tons of grain from us. Canada has failed to show leadership by not suggesting discussions on the problems of transportation, or giving any commitments in that area. Even if we had enough grain there would still be a problem because it cannot be transported.
Even before the problem of transportation, there comes the question of whether we can grow enough grain. Little has been done to encourage improved agricultural production in Canada or in the developed world. The minister did suggest that aid be given to those countries that have shown the greatest degree of mobility in agricultural production. That might seem like a good arrangement at first sight, but really those are the very countries that do not need the food as much as the less developed countries. Starvation is not occurring in those countries that have mobility in agricultural production. That is where the minister suggested our aid should go, but that is not at all really giving in the true sense of giving.
The minister also pointed out that we would be doing more trade with cereal grains under GATT arrangements. One has to question why GATT is involved in the situation at all in view of who the aid recipients are, Mr. Speaker. They are the peoples who spend 80 per cent of their dollar on the purchase of food. Should food be supplied by the developed countries under the protection of GATT? In a sense that is not giving anything at all; it is simply another ploy to use the poor to reap wealth for those who already have.
Kurt Waldheim said we have to double the onslaught on world hunger. We are a long way from that, Mr. Speaker. We are something in excess of 22 million tons short in food reserves at the present time. Food production must greatly increase, yet we see very few incentives for what ought to have taken place.
One of the real situations in which we must see a change is in the concept of world structure. We have talked about aid, but we really need to have a world structure that talks about food, distributed through a system such as a world food bank. Only to give aid away is simply a short-term plan, and not a leadership position. We need something like a world food bank that has a long-term assurance of
World Food Crisis
food and the other advantage, avoiding political ties on a bilateral basis.
If there is anything we need it is something that parallels the International Development Agency of the world bank which allows us to collect on a world basis foodstuffs to feed the hungry and distribute them without any political association on a priority basis according to the needs of people.
That was not the government's commitment at the conference in Rome. What it is telling us is that it is going to be giving food to those who have shown the highest degree of mobility in their own agriculture. I suggest that that will not do very much to lower the rate of starvation and malnutrition as it is presently experienced on the planet earth. The situation is extremely serious. In this debate today we are not just talking about the situation that exists at the Rome conference. The motion before us states:
That this House condemns the government for its failure, both before and during the World Food Conference in Rome-
The key words are "before and during." We have experienced LIFT. It would have been more appropriately called GOOF.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE LEADERSHIP IN SOLVING WORLD FOOD CRISIS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE LEADERSHIP IN SOLVING WORLD FOOD CRISIS
speechtext:
How in the world could we possibly have had an agricultural policy in this country within the past three or four years that talked about not growing grain? Surely the relevant figures have been before us for something in excess of two decades. Scientists have told us for a considerable period of time what was going to happen, yet in this country, in 1974, we find it acceptable to bury millions of surplus eggs and kill cattle in protest.
The government has not taken the full responsibility before or during the food conference in talking about the need for food and giving it to those who need it most. The situation is extremely serious.
Another area we heard nothing about at this conference, either before or after, concerns what is to be the Canadian or North American role in terms of our consumption of food. That is a question that needs a response. The fact of the matter is that one of the very critical factors that affects the supply of food in the world today is the amount in excess of their need that people in the developed countries are consuming.
One piece of research states that economists and food experts suggest that probably the central theme of the World Food Conference ought to be that Americans and other affluent people had better eat less or face the confrontation of half a billion hungry people.
To give an example, the United States spends more money on pet food than on foreign aid. And I am not going to suggest that Canada is very much better off. We also see other situations. More money is spent in North America putting fertilizer on lawns and golf courses than is used in the whole third world.
With these kinds of problems it is not enough to go to Rome and make a promise. This is a case where we must have a personal commitment; it has to be a commitment from us. We cannot maintain that our standard is right

November 15, 1974
World Food Crisis
and that we will help only to the extent of our own comfort. If we are to be at all giving, we must give of ourselves as well as giving tangible objects.
North Americans consume directly or indirectly five times as much cereal grain, a principal source of protein, as the average citizen of Latin America, Asia or Africa. When we talk about aid it is important that we do it in terms of reducing our own consumption of food. Putting it in perspective with the minister's statement today I wish to share with this House information that shows the smallness of our commitment in Rome.
It has been estimated that if Canadians ate one less hamburger per week, one million extra tons of grain would be available to feed an additional five million people. The commitment the Canadian people gave in Rome was equivalent to one hamburger per week. I suggest that is a pretty trifling contribution to make to a world that has needs that are so great.
I have tremendous respect for the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Hogan). I respect him for bringing this motion before the House. I differ with him on one position he took. He said that population is not the problem, it is the people and their rate of consumption. To put it in a more correct perspective, consumption has to be seen as very important, but paralleled with it must be the population explosion.
If consumption is the problem, who is it that is consuming all this stuff except people? Obviously it has to be a people problem. The hon. member quoted from Scientific American to illustrate his point. Another article on page 43 states, and I quote:
In accordance with the same law of geometric progression, the human population has reached its present size through comparatively few doublings. Even if we again assume that humanity began with a hypothetical Adam and Eve, the population has doubled only 31 times, or an average of about once every 30,000 years.
The fact is we now know that population doubles every 28 years, even though the historical average is something like every 30,000 years.
I suggest that at the conference of Rome there is not enough talk about incentives for decreasing population, or at least stabilizing world population. There can be no hope for humanity if we do not reverse the trend of filling the earth plumb full of human beings. The balance of the ecology simply will not accept that kind of filling up. The earth cannot support it. One of the things that must happen is that we must accept a whole new attitude about food.
I have asked questions of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) about whether there was ever to be a guaranteed nutritive analysis attached to human foodstuffs. That question has relevance because of the fact that when we go into supermarkets today tc buy weiners or bologna, we assume we are buying protein. The fact is in many cases we could buy cheaper protein if we bought roasts or steaks.
It becomes important that we put nutritive values on foods because we need to start educating people to think differently about food. The sale of food products is based on taste, colour and style. We have to realize that the food shortage we talk about in the world is not really a general food shortage. There is enough carbohydrate to go around.

What this world is experiencing is a protein shortage, and a transportation shortage. There is not enough protein; there is not enough transportation.
The government must ask Canadians to set the example. Canadians should be asked to change the amount that they use in luxury foods for pets. The amount we throw away or waste each year is enough to feed a major portion of those who are starving. When I say we, I mean all North Americans. When you note that the United States spends more money on pet food than foreign aid, something is seriously wrong.
Something else that is critical when talking about the "before and after" of this motion is that the government has done virtually nothing to preserve the resources that allow us to produce food. There are only two sources for the production of food, soil and water.
All across this country we see the deplorable situation where acres upon acres of high quality food-producing soil are being taken out of production. The federal government may suggest that is a provincial responsibility and that it has no obligations in that field. However, that is not so.
I give just one example out of a large number which might have been chosen. A decision was taken to build a satellite airport encompassing 1,445 acres near the community of Villeneuve, North of Edmonton. Three sites were available. The site chosen covered 50 per cent class one soil and 45 per cent class two soil. Mr. Speaker, many countries in the world do not have class one or class two soil. An alternative site was available three miles to the west which would have used class five and class seven land only-class five soil is non-improvable pasture, and class seven is non-agricultural.
Every year in this country large tracts of agricultural land are being removed from production to the extent that by the turn of the century it is estimated 50 per cent of the highest grades of soil will have been destroyed. At the present time there are virtually no incentives forthcoming to reverse this trend. How serious is it? According to soil science professors at the University of Alberta it is serious to the extent that, if the present trend continues and if the Canadian population doubles by the year 2,000, as predicted, this country will have great difficulty in feeding itself, let alone building up reserves of grain to distribute to the developing countries.
To give another example. In the last seven years the City of Edmonton has expanded over agricultural land, 19,438 acres of which were in the top two soil classes. That amount of land would easily have raised 80 million bushels of wheat over the next hundred years. I speak in terms of a century, but the anthropologists tell us that man has been on this earth for some 50,000 years. I am sure that cities would not be allowed to spread over this kind of acreage if, underneath the land, were tarsands, nickel, iron ore or any of the other resources we consider to be of value today. There is simply not enough attention being given to food production in this country and in the world generally. This, also, is a subject which calls for leadership.
In summary, while I realize the government would like to take pleasure and pride in what has been achieved so far, I do not believe it can properly do so. The minister
November 15, 1974

said that the mover of this motion used language which was excessive, irresponsible and deplorable. I would reply by saying that anyone who reads today's Hansard will realize that a lot of information has been put on record today. It certainly was not irresponsible to show concern for those in the developing countries where between 400 million and 800 million people are suffering from malnutrition. And it can hardly be called excessive to ask that more should be given, when the pets of North America live in circumstances far better than any which exist for the greater part of the human community.
The cause is mankind; the need is great. The country must go beyond platitudes and talks concerning agreements on tariffs and trade, if it is to show leadership. We cannot expect people who have nothing to get their food through trade arrangements with the rich. I think that the government's position is deplorable, is excessive, and that it is irresponsible.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE LEADERSHIP IN SOLVING WORLD FOOD CRISIS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to put forward a few points of view in this debate. I had intended to begin by congratulating the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Hogan) for expressing his concern on this subject, and for bringing this matter to the attention of the House. I must say, though, that I question how seriously he or his party are committed to this motion when I see Only one member of his group in attendance in the House.

speechtext:
I should like to make a few comments which may appear to be somewhat apart from the core of the question we have been considering. I believe the government should be commended on the stand it has taken, the concern it has shown and the commitment it has made in this situation where millions in the undeveloped countries of the world are facing starvation.
It appears to be the wish of many people that Canada should make a very large commitment of grain to help meet these circumstances. This, in my view, is commendable. After all, Canada grows a lot of grain. Grain is a product which has a long shelf life; it can be used almost directly for human consumption, or indirectly through livestock feeding. But this raises another issue.
We in this House are aware that from time to time food surpluses arise in this country, and there is a disposition to send these surpluses to under-developed countries should it be possible to do so. For example, in the riding I represent there was, recently, a surplus of potatoes which had been damaged by frost. These potatoes are unacceptable to the Canadian table trade. One of the solutions might be to have them made into flakes or instant mash, which might then be made available to the world food program. When I looked at the arithmetic involved, though, I realized how expensive it is to proceed with this type of approach.
Canada could, perhaps, be offering many of these other food items but it is not possible to do so because of the very high cost of processing and packaging-the packag-
World Food Crisis
ing is necessary in order that the product may be distributed without waste, spoilage, or, perhaps, pilferage, after it reaches its destination. When the government is considering making funds available for food relief programs I trust it will not ignore the need for storage refrigerators and an adequate distribution system within the countries we are trying to help. Without doing this we are restricted to commodities such as grain that require no refrigeration and can be distributed through very low quality systems.
I listened with interest last evening to the representative of the Canadian Wheat Board who appeared before the agricultural committee. He put forward a view I think we would do well to reflect upon, Mr. Speaker. He made the point that world population is increasing at the rate of 2.5 per cent to 3 per cent a year, as the hon. member opposite mentioned, but that world food production is increasing at only 2 per cent to 2.5 per cent a year. So it appears world food production is falling behind the gain in population.
This official put forward what I thought was a rather interesting viewpoint. He said the problem for the future will be related more to the cyclical nature of food production rather than the total amount of food production. It was his point of view, if I interpreted it correctly, that there would be periods of severe food shortage, as we are now experiencing, whereas at other times we may have a very high inventory as a result of good crop years. This leads me to agree with the previous speaker who said one of the things we should seriously consider is the establishment of a world food bank, so that when grain and other commodities are available in some quantity they can be stored and handled by a central agency, and be available in real time of need without disrupting the economies of the food producing countries.
One question has been avoided by a number of members who have addressed themselves to this problem, and now perhaps is the time to raise it, and I do so on a personal basis. It seems to me it would go a long way toward correcting some of the difficulties that have been referred to if refrigeration facilities, storage facilities, transportation facilities and distribution facilities were substantially funded.
Perhaps this might be a good investment for some of the countries today that are accumulating large amounts of world currency. Generally speaking, these countries-I speak particularly of the OPEC nations-are not major food producers, and through this medium they would offer direct assistance. In addition, many other countries could respond very vigorously in supplying expertise. I hope that in fulfilling our commitment of large grain shipments, both now and in the next three years, we will not ease up on sending to the needy countries those people in Canada who can do so much in helping them become more self-sufficient. In this regard I sincerely applaud the opening remarks of the minister; nothing could be more true.
Irrespective of the commitment of this country or any other country, the end solution has to be self-sufficiency in as many countries as possible. As I say, the best way of achieving this is to provide expertise, and I think in this

regard Canada has something to offer in terms of research into grain production, growing and harvesting.
The question was raised this morning of why we were not sending more fertilizer to the third world. In my past occupations I have had some experience with the fertilizer industry and its problems, and I have reservations about whether this is a very viable suggestion. I am surprised that the mover of the motion we are now debating did not make the point that we should contribute toward building fertilizer plants in countries of need. I think what escaped the hon. member was how very expensive fertilizer is, if it is manufactured in this country or the United States, by the time it gets to the third world. How much more economical it would be if they had their own fertilizer plants and we shipped the necessary ingredients to them.
This brings me to another area that is even wider. Any country that is hopeful of a real future must be self-sufficient both in energy and in food. Unfortunately, at the present time, with trends in pricing set by many factors of the sort we have been discussing during the last couple of weeks, the price of food and energy on the world markets is accelerating at a rapid rate. This puts the underdeveloped nations in a much less favourable position than they ever were before.
I am sure all Canadians, as most other people, sincerely want to do the best they can to assist in the present crisis, but what is so disheartening to them is that things are getting worse, and probably will continue to get worse since the underdeveloped countries are becoming increasingly incapable of purchasing food, fertilizer and energy. As I say, if they are to have any hope of a future we must address ourselves to the question of how we can narrow the gap.
I was quite impressed with the remarks of the previous speaker, not only with what he said and the manner in which he said it, but in terms of the attitude that he said some countries we are trying to help adopt in relation to population trends. This question embraces more than simply consumption of food and food availability; it is a question, addressed to the whole world, of the capability of the world to meet food demands.
Somewhere the two points of food production and world demand will meet on the graph and cross. A number of speakers have indicated that perhaps this point in time is not that far into the future and no amount of talk is going to change that. As we are approaching this point we must recognize that, if we want to live on this earth in peace and give the underdeveloped countries hope for the future, we must address ourselves to these two questions of world food demand and the capability of the world to produce that food.
I do not want to talk about energy today, but in relation to the food crisis there is an old saying which is quoted many times, that a hungry man knows no God and knows no boundary. If we cannot effectively solve the present problem and give these hungry people hope for a final resolution of their problem, then we will be facing a much larger problem some time in the future. That is why it is terribly important to take action now.
One very important point that the minister mentioned, and which I want to adopt, is that despite the crisis we are

facing today, and the very generous offer Canada has made to help to the best of our ability, the key to the problem is to make the third world as self-sufficient as possible in terms of food production. In this regard those nations too have some responsibility to do something about their population trends.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have had a very good debate this afternoon on the World Food Conference and the situation in the world generally. The case has been very well put forth by the opposition parties, and we have heard a defence on the part of the government of what it has done and contributed.
I should like to say a little bit about what the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) has outlined as one of the concerns of the World Food Conference in Rome, and that is in respect of the supply of food, or the lack of it. This afternoon the minister was very thin skinned and felt that Canada had made a tremendous contribution. I do congratulate the government for what it has done, but I think it should do more in relation to the amount of agricultural production we have in Canada.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) in his speech in Rome, and I take this out of context, said that what is obviously needed now is a world agricultural policy, and there is not one. I would say the same thing to the government of Canada, and the producers in Canada have been saying this for a number of years. What is obviously needed in Canada is an agricultural policy, and there is not one.
In 1968 and 1969 we had an agricultural congress which was supposed to develop an agricultural policy for Canada. We still do not have an agricultural policy, due mainly to the lack of leadership on the part of the government over the years. I suggest that the agricultural congress was held as the result of producers in Canada saying the government had adopted a cheap food policy, a policy of bringing cheap food into the country from anywhere in the world to compete with our producers, putting them out of production. I suggest that that is what is taking place in the beef industry today, and as a result of this policy Canada is now a net importer of food.
We are only producing at about half throttle. We certainly should be concerned about lack of food supplies when countries such as Canada are not producing at full throttle, particularly in light of the present situation in the world in which the peoples of some countries have no food at all.
The argument that we are not really producing as much as we can in Canada can be well documented. We have had many programs in the past few years aimed at reducing or halting production. Whenever we have had a surplus of production we have faced a real problem in disposing of the surplus. I suggest that problem has been aggravated by the policy of this country to import cheap food. This has resulted in a lack of faith on the part of our producers, hence they are hesitant about going into high gear in the production of food. No one can argue with the suggestion that we are not producing as much food in Canada as we

couJd. If we are going to get production into high gear in Canada we must develop programs to take care of surpluses.
Some hon, members have referred to a world food bank. Such a program could not operate unless we had means to take care of surplus production. I have never felt it would be wrong to have a year's supply of grain in storage in Canada. Very often we see weather changes that inhibit production, and this is true of almost every farm commodity.
Very often shortages of supply can be related to programs that inhibit production. We must have a program to take care of over-production such as we have in beef at this time. Our production structure should not be such that it creates bad faith on the part of beef producers, and that is the situation today. Beef producers are reducing their basic herds, and before long this will result in an under-production which will do nothing at all in our effort to help feed the people of the world.
There are many people who will ask how we can afford to feed needy people, or if we can afford it at all. I suggest that we can to some extent by using the money that we are now using for programs such as LIP. The taxpayers of this country are paying a great deal of money in the way of unemployment insurance benefits because of high unemployment. If we adopted a program of constructing canneries and granaries to take care of agricultural surpluses we would put a lot of unemployed to work, cutting down on high unemployment and on taxes required for unemployment insurance benefits. Many people who are working on programs such as LIP could be put to work in more productive areas, and I suggest that what will precipitate such a change is a crisis such as the food shortage.
We hear a lot about change, and many books have been written about it, such as "Future Shock". We hear a great deal about how people will have to change because of manufacturing devices that put people out of work. The biggest change in our outlook in Canada and, indeed, on the North American continent, is the change in respect of producing enough food to feed the world. I suggest we will have to stop wasting fertilizer, sprays and that type of thing, and here I think of the waste in respect of lawns, gardens and golf courses. We will need that fertilizer to produce food.
The hon. member for Peel-Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Milne) suggested that we should construct fertilizer manufacturing plants in other countries. I cannot subscribe to that idea. If we build more plants of this type we should build them in Canada, close to the source of the raw material. In this way we would create more jobs for our unemployed here.
If we have to give others the product I think that is much better than giving it to people in our own country and teaching them how not to work. For instance, Mr. Speaker, we have the raw material here. We know there is an abundant supply of potash. We also know that if energy is required in order to produce fertilizer, we have that energy.
We also know that when there was an increase in the manufacture of fertilizer in western Canada several years
World Food Crisis
ago, quite a lot of the increase was based on agricultural production of the day. However, just as companies were building plants in order to increase the production of fertilizer we had the LIFT program which took a lot of land out of the production of grain. Because the companies were building plants it was necessary for them to sell their production in order to have a source of income. Since the production of grain was being reduced, the product was exported out of Canada.
Last year the government told us that the way to beat inflation was to produce. When we asked about a shortage in fertilizer we were assured that there would not be a shortage, but of course we know from experience that there was a shortage. We also know that a large proportion of fertilizer production was exported from Canada. I do not blame the fertilizer companies because it is obvious they cannot pay for their plants if there is insufficient production.
We know that, because of the price of fertilizer over a number of years, it was really not profitable to develop some of the raw materials we had in Canada. These were imported into Canada more cheaply. However, with the price of fertilizer what it is today there should be programs to urge fertilizer manufacturers in Canada to use some of the basic minerals we have, and develop them so that there will be a greater supply of fertilizer products manufactured in Canada from basic materials within Canada.
So, Mr. Speaker, I am sure in the next few years a new outlook must be developed in this whole area. We can see ourselves having to accept a much lower standard of living, perhaps not too much lower, but certainly a lower standard of living. I believe we in Canada have an obligation to produce more in the agricultural field, and to do a better job than we are doing now in feeding the world.

Mr. Speaker, in the four remaining minutes-I just lost 30 seconds-I would also like to join with those who spoke before me in thanking the mover for the opportunity he gave the minister to right the impressions the World Food Conference had left in Rome.
It is quite obvious that the motion introduced by the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Hogan) was based on doubtful information, information gathered from doubtful sources. Perhaps, he could have gone deeper into things and inquired of the personnel of the department about what really happened, instead of listening to the catch lines, as the minister called them, that spread all sorts of falsehoods about the position of the government of Canada in Rome. Nevertheless, Mr. Speaker, it is a clear improvement on the motion discussed Tuesday and introduced by the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner), and which was in fact another one of his witch hunts, and it is quite typical of that member to find dishonest people and criminals all over the place. Some were even found in this House of Commons.
Mr. Speaker, the information and explanations given by the minister will nevertheless right the facts. Canada was the country which took a position of initiative, of leadership, about the problems facing developing countries. I am

somewhat disappointed, Mr. Speaker. However, I would like to say in the remaining seconds what I would have liked to have enough time to say in a more specific and elaborate way. I was somewhat disappointed that nobody dealt with the cause of the problems facing those African countries. I am talking about countries faced with starvation, more particularly Niger, Mauritania, Upper Volta, Sahel, Bali, Chad, and Senegal.
Mr. Speaker, it is all a series of disasters after disasters which brought about that situation in those unfortunate countries. I heard hon. members of the opposition blame the government for its lack of planning. There is nothing more difficult to plan than agricultural production, food production, because one is always at the mercy of the elements. How can one be sure things will work out exactly as planned, as wanted, as foreseen if, as we have
noticed in the countries mentioned earlier, in that central strip of Africa there are calamities, floods and droughts?
Somehow, I am sorry, Mr. Speaker, that those problems were not dealt with adequately. My colleague from Ottawa West (Mr. Francis) barely touched upon the subject when he mentioned the phenomenon of the weather which, in fact, cripples us in any serious undertaking. I am sorry, Mr. Speaker, but unfortunately it is five o'clock.
